analysis.title: The New Defense Economy (Tales from the Emerging World, Emerging Markets Equity Team, November 2026)
key_insights: Global military spending hit a record $2.9 trillion in 2025. NATO's European members and Canada raised spending 20% in a single year, the highest growth since 1953. Europe's military spending rose 14% in 2025.
Poland spends 4.5% of GDP on defense, the largest share in the alliance. Polish arms imports were nine times higher in 2021-2025 than in 2016-2020.
At the 2025 Hague summit, NATO members committed to spending 5% of GDP on defense and related security requirements by 2035.

Industrial capacity now constrains defense as much as budgets do. NATO's procurement agency says ammunition deliveries to Ukraine can take 24 to 36 months, and the UK's 155mm shell production ramp has been delayed by at least six months, with full operation expected in 2027. The team expects Europe's catch-up cycle to be long and uneven.

The team sees an investment theme beyond the traditional U.S. defense complex. Europe drives demand, while some of the most interesting supply-side beneficiaries are in emerging markets, where exporters offer capability, speed and lower costs.

Drones have lowered the cost of combat. Ukraine's monthly FPV drone production capacity rose from 20,000 in 2024 to 200,000 in 2025, with a plan to reach 600,000 in 2026. U.S. NDAA earmarks about $1.7 billion for small unmanned aerial systems, more than four times 2022 spending but under 1% of the defense budget.
Conventional platforms remain the backbone of forces and receive most new spending. The report expects drones to be paired with conventional forces that need depth and replenishment.

South Korea is described as one of the more credible EM beneficiaries. It offers tanks, self-propelled artillery, missiles, ammunition and armored vehicles with shorter delivery times and often lower prices than comparable Western systems, and its industry sits within a Western-aligned security framework.

South Korean defense exports rose from roughly $7.3 billion in 2021 to $15.4 billion in 2025. Poland accounted for about 46% of 2025 exports. The next phase depends on continued order inflows and the pace of rearmament among NATO, Indo-Pacific and Middle East partners.

Brazil is a smaller, specialized story: military transport aircraft (the C-390 Millennium, flying with several NATO members), rocket artillery and armored vehicles. Its role is expected to stay more specialized than South Korea's.

India is not yet an export power and still relies on Russia, France, Israel and others for advanced systems. It approved the purchase of 114 Rafales in February. The more investable areas are expected to be electronics, radars, sensors, missiles and ammunition, through import substitution, but procurement is bureaucratic and execution is the challenge.

The U.S. remains the dominant defense supplier, spender and exporter of advanced systems. Buyers still want U.S. equipment but also want local support, faster delivery and contract assurance, which creates room for EM suppliers in categories where speed, affordability and supply assurance matter.

sector_views.rationale: Europe's rearmament creates a demand shock and replenishment cycle. Select EM exporters, mainly South Korea, gain share on speed, scale and price.
Continuous domestic procurement, scale, shorter delivery times and lower prices drove exports from $7.3B in 2021 to $15.4B in 2025.
Specialized platforms with a maturing opportunity. The report says it lacks South Korea's breadth and scale.
Localization is a policy priority, but execution and technology gaps limit the opportunity. Opportunities are selective (electronics, radars, sensors, missiles, ammunition).
